title: How I Edit a 20-Minute Talking Head Video in Under an Hour
creator: Nadia Reyes Edits
description:
My full workflow for editing long talking-head videos fast: folder setup, the rough cut, a two-node color grade, audio cleanup and export settings.

Framecut (sponsor): 25% off with code EDITFAST at https://framecut.ai/editfast

My LUTs: https://nadiareyes.co/luts
Camera: Sony a7 IV, Sigma 24-70

sentences.t: If you make long talking-head videos, you know the edit is the part that eats your whole week.
I used to spend like six hours on a twenty-minute video, and today I'm going to show you how I get that under an hour.
This is the actual footage from my last upload, so you're seeing the real thing, not a demo project.
Step one is boring but it matters, folders.
Every project gets the same four folders, A-roll, B-roll, audio and exports, and I name them exactly the same every single time.
That way my templates always find the right files and I'm not hunting around for clips.
I also record a clap at the start of every take, because syncing audio by hand is a nightmare.
Okay, step two, and this is where most of the time used to go, the rough cut.
For the rough cut I'm dropping the whole A-roll into Framecut, so that's about thirty-five minutes of me talking.
It transcribes everything in about a minute, and now my footage is basically a text document.
So here at the start I said the intro three times, and I'm just going to highlight the first two attempts and hit delete.
And you can see the timeline on the right just cut those out.
Now I'll click remove silences and set the threshold to about half a second, because I like to keep a little bit of breathing room.
That took the whole thing from thirty-five minutes down to twenty-two, and I haven't touched a single clip yet.
Then I scroll through and kill the ums and the tangents, like this whole bit where I talk about my cat for no reason.
And I export it as an XML so it opens straight into my main editor with every cut intact.
So that whole rough cut took me about seven minutes, which used to be two or three hours of scrubbing.
Okay, real quick, Framecut is actually sponsoring this video, so let me tell you about it.
If you edit anything with a lot of talking, podcasts, tutorials, interviews, it's honestly a game changer.
It works with Premiere, Resolve and Final Cut, and there's a free plan if you just want to try it on one project.
And if you want the full version, use my code EDITFAST for twenty-five percent off your first year at framecut.ai slash editfast.
The link is down in the description.
Alright, back in my editor, step three is color.
I keep it really simple, two nodes.
The first node is just exposure and white balance, getting my skin tone where it should be.
I always check skin on the vectorscope, you want it sitting right along that skin tone line.
The second node is my look, which is a soft film LUT at about forty percent strength.
Because I shoot in the same room with the same lights every time, I can copy this grade to every clip and I'm basically done.
That's the whole secret, honestly, the less you change on set, the less you fix in the edit.
Step four, audio.
I run a noise reduction pass first, very light, because heavy noise reduction makes you sound like you're underwater.
Then a compressor so the loud bits and quiet bits are closer together, and a limiter at minus one so nothing clips.
I aim for around minus fourteen loudness, which is roughly where YouTube normalizes anyway.
And I drop a little room tone under any hard cuts so the background doesn't suddenly go dead silent.
Step five, export.
H.264, the same frame rate I shot at, and a high bitrate, around forty megabits for 4K.
People overthink export settings so much, but YouTube is going to recompress it anyway, so just give it a clean, high-quality file.
And that's it, folders, rough cut, two-node color, audio and export, and the whole thing took me fifty-two minutes today.
If you've got a workflow trick I didn't mention, put it in the comments, I read all of them.
I'll see you in the next one.
